messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rohan, a 29-year-old painter of South Asian descent, had always been proud of his ability to navigate the streets of New York City with ease. However, that confidence was shattered one night when he was mugged on his way home from work. The sudden and violent attack left him shaken, and in the months that followed, Rohan began to experience a growing sense of unease. It started with dreams – vivid, disturbing nightmares that would leave him gasping for breath as he woke up. Waking up from these nightmares, Rohan felt like he was still on edge, his body tense and ready to react to any perceived danger. These episodes of "dream residue" would trigger a cascade of emotions, making him irritable and quick to anger. He would lash out at his wife, Nalini, or get into heated arguments with his clients over minor issues – a far cry from the patient and understanding person he used to be. As Rohan navigated the city streets for work, certain physical locations would suddenly transport him back to that fateful night. The sight of a dark alleyway or the sound of footsteps behind him would send his mind racing, making him feel like he was reliving the trauma all over again. These spatial triggers would also bring forth fragments of memories – fleeting images and sounds that only served to heighten his sense of unease. Rohan struggled to recall the events of that night with any clarity. He remembered being grabbed from behind, but the details were hazy. When he tried to deliberately remember what happened, he found it difficult to access the memory, as if his mind was actively blocking it out. This incomplete picture only added to his feelings of guilt and self-blame – why couldn't he recall more? Why had he been so careless? As Rohan's memories continued to haunt him, he began to see the world in a different light. He started to mistrust strangers, wondering if they were hiding ulterior motives behind their friendly smiles. He felt isolated from his friends and family, unable to connect with them on a deeper level. Nalini tried to reassure him, but Rohan couldn't shake off the feeling that he was completely alone in this struggle. This growing sense of mistrust and isolation only heightened Rohan's threat response. His body remained constantly tense, scanning his surroundings for potential dangers. He became hypervigilant, always on the lookout for signs of danger – a suspicious glance from a passerby or an unexpected noise. This state of perpetual alertness was exhausting, leaving him drained and irritable. As Rohan's negative appraisals continued to shape his worldview, he began to see himself as a victim – someone who couldn't rely on others to keep him safe. This self-perception only served to reinforce his threat response, creating a vicious cycle of fear and hypervigilance. He started avoiding certain areas of the city, fearing that he would be targeted again. The consequences of Rohan's avoidance behaviors began to accumulate. His business suffered as he turned down jobs in "risky" neighborhoods, and his relationships with Nalini and their friends grew strained. Despite her best efforts to reassure him, Rohan couldn't shake off the feeling that he was losing control – that the world around him was spiraling into chaos. As the months went by, Rohan's symptoms only intensified. He knew he needed help, but his pride and fear of being seen as weak held him back. It wasn't until Nalini staged an intervention, begging him to seek professional help, that Rohan finally realized he couldn't face this alone. With a mix of trepidation and hope, he began the journey towards healing – one that would require him to confront his deepest fears and learn to trust again.
